name: Street Custom 'Backfire' Weaponized Exhaust System
description: A vehicle-mounted improvised weapon created by modifying a motorcycle or small vehicle's exhaust system to inject raw fuel into the exhaust manifold on command, producing a jet of flame from the tailpipe that extends 3-5 meters behind the vehicle. The modification is simple — a secondary fuel injector spliced into the exhaust pipe with a dashboard trigger — and has become common enough in Tier 1 and 2 vehicle culture that mechanics advertise the conversion openly. It is primarily a pursuit deterrent, used to discourage tailgating vehicles and on-foot pursuers, but the flame output is sufficient to cause severe burns and ignite clothing or fuel leaks.
specifications:
flame range: 3-5 meters behind vehicle
fuel consumption: 2 liters per 10-second burst
ignition: Spark plug in exhaust manifold
installation time: 2-3 hours with basic tools
weight: 3 kg additional hardware
fuel source: Vehicle's primary fuel tank or auxiliary reservoir
fire duration: Limited by fuel supply
story_hooks: A street racing fatality involved a Backfire system that was remotely triggered — someone hacked the driver's ignition circuit and cooked the rider behind them.
A convoy of modified vehicles with Backfire systems has been running protection for smuggling routes — the wall of fire behind the convoy makes pursuit effectively impossible.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutalist mechanical retrofit—a secondary fuel injector assembly grafted onto an existing exhaust manifold, all raw industrial aggression. The core is a modified fuel line with a thumb-sized solenoid valve body, branching from the main exhaust pipe like a parasite. No elegance, pure function: this is street mechanics' work, visible and unapologetic.
physical_description.dimensions: Injector body: 12 cm length × 8 cm width × 6 cm height. Secondary fuel line: 40-60 cm run to manifold. Dashboard trigger housing: 7 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm (mounted separately).
physical_description.weight_description: The injector itself is light—under 1 kg—but installation adds structural mass to the exhaust system. Feels heavy in concept rather than hand; the real weight is mechanical burden on the vehicle frame.
physical_description.primary_material: Cast aluminum solenoid housing with stainless steel fuel lines. Carbon-steel manifold clamps. Polymer-sheathed electrical harness. Ignition spark plug assembly (ceramic and copper).
physical_description.finish: Raw aluminum with oxidation streaks. Stainless lines show welding discoloration—blues and oranges from heat treatment. Clamps are bare metal, already showing surface rust in high-humidity GLMZ environments. No protective coating; this is built to work, not to last.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray (aluminum), silver-orange (welded steel), black electrical harness. Fuel line interior visible through transparent sections—amber or clear polymer tubing.
physical_description.grip_texture: N/A for primary assembly. Dashboard trigger is rubberized polymer with a grooved thumb plate, engineered for gloved operation—crucial for drivers wearing tactical or augmented gloves.
distinctive_features: Solenoid valve with audible click on activation—an acoustic signature that precedes the flame
Visible spark plug ceramic tip mounted in exhaust manifold shroud
Secondary fuel line junction marked with hand-welded solder joints and mechanical crimp fittings
Dashboard trigger wired with exposed conduit in many installations—no cable sheathing
Heat scorching on clamps and mounting points from repeated ignitions—discolored metallurgy telling the story of use
Faint fuel residue residue stains along fuel line runs
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Street Custom etched or stamped on the solenoid housing in crude lettering. Serial numbers (if present) are often ground off or defaced—this is a prohibited modification. Solenoid brand names may be visible (aftermarket industrial part). Dashboard trigger has no marking; it's typically a generic push-button enclosure.
physical_description.condition_typical: Field-worn and improvised. Mounting clamps show vibration looseness. Fuel line connections exhibit minor weeping—not leaks, but the slow seep of constant pressure. Spark plug ceramic shows carbon buildup and heat discoloration. Dashboard trigger often has a sticker or electrical tape reinforcement where the activation wire enters the housing. This is a modification that degrades with every use; mechanics expect to service it monthly.
